description: We are a group of Biomed and Computer Student Engineers & Space Enthusiasts!
summary:
To enable autonomous health monitoring on long-duration missions, astronauts need advanced tools to evaluate deep-tissue, bone, and neurological changes. While current sensors track essential vitals, diagnosing complex internal shifts requires Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). To help realize this capability, we developed the Space MRI Virtual Prototype Engine.

Because space-compatible MRIs do not exist yet, our software uses Model-Based Systems Engineering to simulate one. Users can interactively design a scanner, balance spacecraft constraints (SWaP), and inject raw NASA SAMS-II vibration telemetry to generate predicted medical images. By simulating this diagnostic technology, we provide the predictive engineering groundwork for future deep-tissue health monitoring in space.
details:
Space MRI Virtual Prototype Engine

What it does and how it works

Our project is a physics-driven simulation platform—a predictive Virtual Prototype—that evaluates how a portable Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scanner would perform aboard the International Space Station (ISS). Because a space-compatible MRI does not exist yet, we use Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) to simulate its operation. The core is a Digital Signal Processing (DSP) engine. It takes an ideal, ground-truth brain MRI and transforms it into the frequency domain (K-space) using a 2D Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). It then applies two main physics-based degradation models:

  1. Low-Field Rician Noise: Simulates the poor Signal-to-Noise Ratio of ultra-low magnetic fields (B0) required for spaceflight.
  2. Motion Artifacts: Injects raw acceleration telemetry from NASA's Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS-II) database, translating ISS microgravity vibrations (e.g., from crew exercise) into K-space phase errors. Finally, an inverse FFT reconstructs the degraded image, generating a visual prediction of the space scan.

What benefits it has & the intended impact

Long-duration missions expose astronauts to severe physiological changes, including bone loss and Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS). Surface-level wearables cannot detect these deep-tissue and neurological shifts. The intended impact of our project is to lay the predictive engineering groundwork for bringing MRI technology to space. By simulating this diagnostic tool, we provide a framework that could eventually empower astronauts to autonomously monitor and evaluate their deep-tissue health. Furthermore, as a Virtual Prototype, it allows researchers to test hardware feasibility before NASA spends millions of dollars on physical prototypes.

How our project is creative

Instead of building a standard dashboard that merely displays health metrics or telemetry, we merged aerospace engineering directly with medical imaging physics. Our creativity lies in the fact that we don't just calculate theoretical interference—we visually generate the corrupted medical image. By mapping real NASA SAMS-II vibration data directly into the mathematical K-space of an MRI scan, we created a tangible, interactive "trade-off" game where users can immediately see how space weather and station activities destroy or preserve medical image quality.

Factors our team considered

We heavily focused on the strict engineering trade-offs required for spaceflight. We considered:

  • SWaP Constraints: We implemented mathematical limits for Size, Weight, and Power, ensuring the designed scanner does not exceed the 2,000 W power and volume limits of an ISS EXPRESS Rack.
  • Human Ergonomics: We constrained the minimum bore size to ensure an astronaut's head and the RF coil can physically fit inside the portable scanner.
  • Clinical Viability: We utilized Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) metrics to evaluate if the degraded images remain diagnostically viable for medical personnel.

Tools, coding languages, and software used

  • Core Language: Python 3.10+
  • Physics & Signal Processing: NumPy, SciPy (for FFT and complex array manipulations)
  • Image Analysis: scikit-image (for SSIM and PSNR image quality metrics)
  • Interactive UI: Streamlit (for building the real-time engineering dashboard)
  • Data Integration: Pandas (for parsing CSV telemetry)
  • External Data: NASA SAMS-II Open Data (vibration datasets) and the Open-Notify API (for live ISS orbital tracking).
